title: Stainless Steel (SS): Meaning, Properties, Uses
summary: Learn more about this materials and its different grades available to manufacture.
body_text: Stainless steel is an alloy composed of iron and at least 10.5% chromium for corrosion resistance and durability. The chromium reacts with oxygen to form a thin, stable oxide layer that protects against rust and surface degradation. Nickel, molybdenum, and manganese improve toughness, ductility, and resistance to pitting and oxidation in specific grades. Stainless steel maintains a non-reactive surface, making it suitable for applications requiring hygiene and chemical stability. The material's combination of mechanical strength, heat resistance, and aesthetic appearance supports its use in construction, automotive, medical, and food processing industries. Different grades of stainless steel offer varying balances of properties like corrosion resistance, hardness, and ductility, making SS metal versatile for industrial and structural purposes. The type of steel refers to different categories and grades of steel, including stainless steel, each designed for specific applications. What is Stainless Steel? Stainless steel is an alloy of iron containing at least 10.5% chromium, which gives it exceptional resistance to corrosion. The chromium reacts with oxygen in the environment to form an ultra-thin, stable layer of chromium oxide (Cr₂O₃) on the surface. The passive film acts as a protective barrier that greatly reduces further oxidation or rust formation and self-repairs if damaged. Stainless steel material is used in architecture, medical instruments, food processing, and chemical industries due to its ability to retain strength, formability, and a clean appearance even in harsh environments. The versatility and durability of SS material make it one of the most reliable choices for structural and industrial applications. How is Stainless Steel Made? Stainless steel is produced by melting iron with alloying elements such as chromium, nickel, and molybdenum, typically in an electric arc furnace or induction furnace. Chromium forms a protective oxide layer that resists corrosion, nickel increases toughness and ductility, and molybdenum improves strength and resistance to pitting. Molten steel is refined through Argon Oxygen Decarburization (AOD) or Vacuum Oxygen Decarburization (VOD) to remove impurities and stabilize the alloy composition. The refined metal is cast into slabs, blooms, or billets and then processed through hot and cold rolling to achieve the desired dimensions. Annealing relieves internal stresses and restores corrosion resistance, followed by pickling and polishing to remove surface oxides and produce a bright, clean finish. The stainless steel production process ensures uniform composition and strength through precise control of alloying and refining stages. The stainless process maintains durability, surface quality, and corrosion resistance for industrial and structural applications. Stainless Steel Production Process What are the Advantages of Stainless Steel? The advantages of Stainless Steel are listed below. Corrosion Resistance: Stainless steel resists rust, oxidation, and staining due to the formation of a passive chromium oxide layer that protects its surface from environmental exposure. High Strength : The alloy composition gives certain stainless steel grades high tensile and yield strength, making them suitable for structural applications and heavy-duty equipment. Durability : Many stainless steel grades maintain mechanical integrity under a wide range of temperatures, pressure, and mechanical stress. Aesthetic Appeal : Stainless steel can achieve a bright, reflective surface finish that provides a modern, clean appearance suitable for architectural and decorative purposes. Ease of Maintenance: Stainless steel requires minimal upkeep since its surface resists dirt accumulation and is easily cleaned with simple maintenance practices. Versatility: Stainless steel supports multiple industrial uses (construction, food processing, chemical manufacturing, transportation, and healthcare equipment). Hygienic Properties: Stainless steel advantages feature a smooth, non-porous surface that prevents bacterial buildup, making it ideal for environments that require high sanitation standards in medical and food-handling settings. Recyclability : Stainless steel is 100% recyclable, conserving resources and reducing waste during manufacturing and end-of-life processes. What are the Disadvantages of Stainless Steel? The disadvantages of Stainless Steel are listed below. High Cost: Stainless steel production involves expensive alloying elements (chromium, nickel, and molybdenum), which increase its cost compared to materials (carbon steel or aluminum). Pitting Corrosion: Stainless steel is susceptible to localized corrosion in chloride-rich environments, where pitting occurs due to the breakdown of the protective chromium oxide layer. Difficult Machinability: Stainless steel presents challenges in machining and forming due to its hardness and work-hardening characteristics, requiring specialized tools and slower cutting speeds. Poor Thermal Conductivity: Stainless steel has lower thermal conductivity compared to metals (copper or aluminum), making it less efficient for heat transfer applications. Heavy Weight: Stainless steel has a higher density than materials, including aluminum, which increases weight and limits its use where lightweight construction is required. Expansion Under Heat: Stainless steel exhibits greater thermal expansion than some alternative metals, which causes dimensional changes in high-temperature applications. Surface Contamination Risk: Improper fabrication or cleaning leads to surface contamination, reducing corrosion resistance and appearance quality. What are the Properties of Stainless Steel? The properties of Stainless Steel are listed below. Corrosion Resistance : Stainless steel resists rust and oxidation through a passive chromium oxide film that shields the surface from environmental exposure. Austenitic grades such as 304 and 316 offer excellent corrosion resistance, with 316 containing molybdenum that improves performance in chloride environments, while ferritic grades provide good resistance in less aggressive conditions. Martensitic grades have moderate corrosion resistance but gain higher strength through heat treatment for mechanical applications. High Tensile Strength : Stainless steel exhibits excellent tensile strength and load-bearing capacity. Austenitic grades combine moderate to high strength with superior ductility, ferritic grades provide good strength and dimensional stability, and martensitic steels achieve the highest strength after quenching and tempering. Thermal Conductivity : Stainless steel has lower thermal conductivity than carbon steel, but provides consistent heat distribution in industrial equipment. Ferritic types conduct heat more efficiently than austenitic grades, making them suitable for exhaust systems and heat exchangers. Hardness : Martensitic stainless steels achieve high hardness through heat treatment, ferritic types offer moderate hardness, and austenitic steels have lower hardness but good formability. Ductility and Formability : Stainless steel retains ductility under stress, allowing fabrication into complex shapes. Austenitic grades exhibit the best formability due to their face-centered cubic structure, ferritic steels provide moderate flexibility, and martensitic types are less ductile after heat treatment. Magnetic and Non-Magnetic Behavior : Ferritic and martensitic steels are magnetic because of their body-centered cubic structure, while austenitic steels are non-magnetic in the annealed condition but become slightly magnetic after cold working. Thermal Expansion : Stainless steel expands when heated, with austenitic types showing the highest thermal expansion, while ferritic and martensitic steels exhibit lower rates. What is the Density of Stainless Steel? The density of stainless steel ranges from 7.75 to 8.05 grams per cubic centimeter, depending on alloy composition and crystal structure. Austenitic grades such as 304 and 316 have densities near 8.0 g/cm³, while ferritic and martensitic grades are lower because of their body-centered cubic structure and reduced nickel content. Stainless steel's metallic structure contributes to its stability and load-bearing performance in demanding environments. The material’s strength and stiffness provide resistance to deformation, while its mass can influence vibration behavior in structural applications, increasing reliability in construction, machinery, and heavy industrial components. The combination of density, strength, and durability allows stainless steel to achieve excellent structural efficiency across architectural, engineering, and manufacturing applications. What is the Melting Point of Stainless Steel? The melting point of stainless steel ranges from 1,400 degrees Celsius to 1,530 degrees Celsius, equivalent to 2,550 degrees Fahrenheit to 2,800 degrees Fahrenheit, depending on its alloy composition. Austenitic grades melt near the higher end of the range, while ferritic and martensitic types melt closer to the lower end due to variations in chromium, nickel, and carbon content. The high melting range and strong metallic bonding contribute to stainless steel’s stability and performance in high-temperature environments. Specific heat-resistant austenitic grades maintain strength and structural integrity under prolonged exposure to intense heat, making them ideal for industrial furnaces, exhaust systems, power generation components, and other thermal processing applications. The formation of a protective chromium oxide layer provides additional resistance to oxidation at elevated temperatures, ensuring consistent performance in conditions where alternative materials lose strength or fail. What is the Chemical Composition of Stainless Steel? The chemical composition of stainless steel consists of iron combined with chromium content ranging from 10.5 to 30%, along with varying amounts of nickel, molybdenum, manganese, and carbon. Chromium is the essential alloying element that forms a thin, stable oxide layer on the surface, providing corrosion and oxidation resistance. Nickel increases toughness, ductility, and stability at elevated temperatures and improves corrosion resistance in reducing environments. Molybdenum strengthens resistance against pitting and crevice corrosion in chloride-containing conditions. Manganese acts as a deoxidizer during steelmaking and helps stabilize the austenitic structure. Carbon increases strength and hardness through its influence on the crystal structure, although excessive carbon reduces corrosion resistance by forming chromium carbides. The proportions of the alloying elements define the characteristics of different stainless steel grades. Austenitic grades contain higher nickel and chromium levels, offering superior corrosion resistance and formability. Ferritic grades rely on higher chromium and low carbon for structural stability and oxidation resistance, while martensitic grades contain more carbon to enable hardening and wear resistance. The balance among the alloying elements determines the mechanical performance, corrosion resistance, and application suitability of stainless steel across industrial and structural uses. What is the Structure of Stainless Steel? The structure of stainless steel varies according to its alloy composition and forms three primary types known as austenitic, ferritic, and martensitic. Austenitic stainless steel has a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure that provides high ductility, toughness, and corrosion resistance while remaining non-magnetic in the annealed condition. Ferritic stainless steel has a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure that offers moderate strength, magnetic properties, and corrosion resistance, magnetic properties, and moderate corrosion resistance, along with oxidation resistance for moderate-temperature applications. Martensitic stainless steel possesses a body-centered tetragonal (BCT) structure that develops when high-carbon austenitic steel is rapidly cooled and tempered, resulting in high hardness and strength but reduced ductility. The variation in crystal structure directly influences mechanical behavior, corrosion resistance, and magnetic response. Austenitic types are preferred for applications requiring excellent formability and hygiene, ferritic types are used where thermal stability and magnetism are desired, and martensitic types are selected for wear-resistant tools and mechanical components. The combination of the structural variations makes stainless steel a reliable material across industrial, architectural, and structural applications. What Are Stainless Steel Uses? The uses of Stainless Steel are listed below. Food Industry : Stainless steel is used in food processing equipment, kitchen utensils, and storage containers because it resists corrosion, staining, and bacterial contamination. The non-reactive surface preserves food quality and meets strict hygiene requirements. Medical Devices : Stainless steel is used in surgical instruments, implants, hospital equipment, and sterilization trays due to its strength, biocompatibility, and resistance to repeated sterilization. Stainless steel's smooth surface prevents microbial growth and supports patient safety in medical environments. Construction Materials : Stainless steel is used in structural frameworks, roofing, bridges, and cladding for its durability, corrosion resistance, and visual appeal. Stainless steel maintains structural integrity under environmental stress while requiring minimal maintenance. Automotive Parts : Stainless steel is used in exhaust systems, trims, fuel tanks, and fasteners because it resists heat, pressure, and chemical exposure. Stainless steel's long service life contributes to vehicle reliability and performance. Kitchenware : Stainless steel is used in cookware, cutlery, and appliances for its resistance to rust and ease of cleaning. Stainless steel polished surface offers aesthetic appeal and functional durability. Chemical and Petrochemical Industry : Stainless steel is used in storage tanks, pipelines, and processing equipment where chemical resistance is critical. Grade selection depends on exposure levels to ensure corrosion protection and mechanical stability under high pressure. Architecture and Design : Stainless steel is used in decorative panels, handrails, sculptures, and building facades for its aesthetic value and weather resistance. Stainless steel reflective surface provides a modern appearance while maintaining strength. Marine Applications : Stainless steel is used in shipbuilding, offshore platforms, and marine fittings in austenitic or duplex grades that withstand saltwater exposure and resist pitting corrosion. Energy and Power Generation : Stainless steel is used in selected boiler, heat exchanger, and turbine components where corrosion resistance and temperature performance are required. What is Stainless Steel Used for in Medical Applications? Uses of Stainless Steel in medical applications are listed below. Surgical Instruments : Stainless steel is used in scalpels, forceps, scissors, clamps, and retractors for hardness, precision, and resistance to repeated sterilization. Stainless steel corrosion resistance ensures instruments maintain sharpness and functionality after exposure to disinfectants and steam. Orthopedic Implants : Stainless steel 316L is used in bone plates, screws, and pins due to its high strength, fatigue resistance, and biocompatibility, providing stability during orthopedic procedures. Medical Devices : Many instruments and diagnostic equipment components use stainless steel for structural integrity, corrosion resistance, and durability under repeated use. Dental Equipment : Stainless steel is used in dental instruments, brackets, and wires for formability, corrosion resistance, and biocompatibility, maintaining hygiene and durability through frequent cleaning and sterilization. Hospital Equipment : Furniture, surgical tables, sterilization trays, and bed frames use stainless steel for ease of cleaning and resistance to bacterial growth, ensuring hygienic conditions. Needles and Guide Wires : Stainless steel is employed in hypodermic needles and guide wires for precision, strength, and biocompatibility, while flexible catheter tubing is made from polymer materials. Can Stainless Steel be Used in Medical Implants? Yes, stainless steel can be used in medical implants for temporary or short- to medium-term applications where strength, corrosion resistance, and formability are critical. Medical-grade 316L stainless steel is preferred due to its low carbon content, which increases resistance to intergranular corrosion and ensures biocompatibility. The material is employed in orthopedic implants (bone plates, screws, and fixation devices) that provide mechanical support during the healing process. Stainless steel’s strength and ductility allow complex shapes while maintaining stability under stress. Titanium and its alloys are more frequently used because of their superior long-term corrosion resistance and biological compatibility for permanent implants. What are the Applications of Stainless Steel in Construction? The applications of Stainless Steel in construction are listed below. Reinforcement Bars: Stainless steel is used in reinforcement bars to strengthen concrete structures exposed to moisture, chlorides, or acidic conditions. Stainless steel corrosion resistance extends the service life of bridges, tunnels, and coastal buildings where environmental stress is high. Cladding and Facades: Stainless steel is used in exterior cladding and architectural facades for its durability, corrosion resistance, and visual appeal. Stainless steel maintains structural integrity under temperature fluctuations and increases building aesthetics through reflective or textured finishes. Structural Beams and Columns: Stainless steel is used in beams, columns, and load-bearing frameworks in large buildings and industrial facilities. Stainless steel has high tensile strength and resistance to deformation, supporting stability in areas exposed to vibration, heat, and heavy loads. Handrails and Balustrades: Stainless steel is used in handrails, balustrades, and staircases because it resists wear, provides safety, and maintains an attractive appearance in indoor and outdoor environments. Roofing and Drainage Systems: Stainless steel is used in roofing panels, gutters, and downpipes for its ability to resist corrosion and withstand extreme weather conditions while maintaining performance over extended service periods. Fasteners and Connectors: Stainless steel is used in bolts, screws, and brackets that secure structural components. Its corrosion resistance ensures reliability in humid, marine, and industrial environments. Expansion Joints and Fittings : Stainless steel is used in construction fittings and expansion joints where corrosion resistance and fatigue strength are required to handle movement, pressure, and temperature variations. Bridges and Monuments: Stainless steel is used in bridge components, railings, and monuments where exposure to rain, salt, and pollutants demands long-term durability and low maintenance. What Role does Stainless Steel Play in Automotive Safety Features? Stainless steel plays a valuable role in automotive safety by providing strength, durability, and corrosion resistance in components exposed to harsh conditions. Stainless steel is used in exhaust systems, fasteners, trim, and select reinforcement zones where resistance to heat, moisture, and corrosive gases is critical. Exhaust systems are stable and provide long-term performance due to stainless steel's ability to withstand high temperatures and corrosive emissions. Stainless steel contributes durability and corrosion resistance in selected automotive components exposed to heat and environmental stress, while crash-energy absorption relies primarily on high-strength carbon steels or aluminum alloys. Stainless steel improves specific components where mechanical strength and environmental resistance are essential for safe and reliable vehicle operation, while most vehicle crash structures rely on high-strength carbon steel or aluminum alloys for impact protection. What Are the Benefits of Stainless Steel in Food Packaging? The benefits of stainless steel in food packaging are evident in its hygienic, corrosion-resistant, and non-reactive qualities that protect food integrity during processing, storage, and transport. Stainless steel's smooth, non-porous surface prevents bacterial growth and allows effective cleaning and sterilization, ensuring compliance with strict hygiene standards. The corrosion resistance of stainless steel maintains structural durability when exposed to moisture, salts, and acidic foods, preventing contamination and material degradation. The stainless steel non-reactive nature ensures that no chemical interaction occurs between the packaging and food, preserving flavor, color, and nutritional value. The material’s strength and impact resistance make it suitable for reusable containers, processing tanks, and handling systems, supporting efficiency across industrial operations. The combination of cleanliness, chemical stability, and durability establishes stainless steel as a preferred material for food packaging and storage applications worldwide. What is the Cost of Stainless Steel Compared to Other Metals? The cost of stainless steel compared to other metals ranges from [$ 2,000 to $3,500] per metric ton, higher than carbon steel at $600- to $1,000 and aluminum at [$1,500–2,400]. Carbon steel costs around [$600 to $ 1,000] per metric ton, while aluminum ranges from [$ 1,500 to $2,400] per ton, subject to fluctuations in supply and demand. The higher cost of stainless steel results from the presence of alloying elements (chromium, nickel, and molybdenum), along with energy-intensive refining processes required to achieve corrosion resistance and mechanical strength. Stainless steel delivers long-term economic advantages in applications where durability, hygiene, and minimal maintenance are essential despite the elevated initial expense. Stainless steel's resistance to rust, chemical exposure, and surface wear extends the lifespan of structures, machinery, and medical devices, offsetting the higher upfront cost in environments demanding longevity and reliability. How is Stainless Steel Recycled? Stainless steel is recycled by collecting scrap material from manufacturing plants, construction sites, and consumer products, then processing it through a series of controlled metallurgical stages to recover its full properties. The process begins with sorting the scrap based on magnetic response and approximate composition to ensure consistency in alloy content. The sorted stainless steel is melted in an electric arc furnace, where impurities are removed and alloying elements (chromium, nickel, and molybdenum) are balanced to achieve the desired grade. Refinement through Argon Oxygen Decarburization (AOD) or vacuum treatment ensures precise chemical composition and purity. The molten stainless steel is cast into slabs, billets, or ingots that are later rolled and shaped into new products once refined. The recycling process reduces the need for raw material extraction, minimizes energy use, and supports sustainable manufacturing by maintaining material quality across multiple life cycles. The ability of stainless steel to retain its original strength, corrosion resistance, and durability makes it one of the most sustainable materials in industrial and structural applications. Is Stainless Steel Easier to Mold than Aluminum? No, Aluminum is easier to mold than stainless steel because of its lower melting point, softer texture, and higher malleability, which allow it to form complex shapes under less pressure and lower temperatures. Aluminum melts at 660 degrees Celsius, while stainless steel melts between 1,400 and 1,530 degrees Celsius, making stainless steel more challenging to mold and shape. The softer nature of aluminum enables efficient casting, extrusion, and stamping processes that reduce tooling wear and energy requirements. Stainless steel requires higher forming forces, specialized equipment, and precise temperature control due to its hardness and strength. Stainless steel provides superior durability, corrosion resistance, and wear protection despite being more difficult to mold, making it ideal for applications requiring long-term performance and structural integrity. The Aluminum remains the preferred material for molding processes that prioritize ease of shaping, lower energy use, and lightweight production. Does Stainless Steel Have Higher Abrasion Resistance than Carbon Steel? Yes, martensitic stainless steels can have higher abrasion resistance than many carbon steels due to their high hardness after heat treatment. Martensitic stainless steels, which are high in carbon and are heat-treated, exhibit excellent hardness and wear resistance, making them suitable for components exposed to friction and mechanical wear. Chromium and molybdenum in stainless steel improve corrosion and pitting resistance, which helps maintain surface integrity under abrasive conditions. Austenitic stainless steels (304 or 316) are softer and have lower abrasion resistance than hardened carbon steel . The superior combination of hardness, corrosion resistance, and surface durability in martensitic stainless steels gives them an advantage in high-abrasion environments. Is Stainless Steel More Impact-Resistant than Cast Iron? Yes, stainless steel is more impact-resistant than cast iron. Stainless steel combines strength, ductility, and toughness, allowing it to absorb energy and deform under stress rather than fracture. Gray cast iron is hard but brittle due to its graphite flake structure, which creates points of weakness. Gray cast iron is prone to cracking or shattering under sudden impact or heavy loads. Stainless steel maintains structural integrity under fluctuating mechanical stresses, making it suitable for construction, automotive components, and pressure vessels. The combination of toughness and resistance to brittle failure gives stainless steel a clear advantage in impact-resistant performance over gray cast iron. Does Stainless Steel Have Superior Thermal Insulation Properties Compared to Copper? No, stainless steel does not have superior thermal insulation properties compared to copper. Copper possesses higher thermal conductivity, averaging around 400 watts per meter-kelvin, while stainless steel averages between 14 and 20 watts per meter-kelvin. The high conductivity of copper allows it to transfer heat efficiently, making it the preferred material in applications (heat exchangers, wiring, and cookware). Stainless steel is a poor conductor of heat but is valued for its strength, corrosion resistance, and ability to maintain performance in harsh or corrosive environments. The material's lower thermal conductivity helps in situations where controlled or gradual heat transfer is required (in industrial processing equipment and specific food applications). Stainless steel offers mechanical durability and chemical stability that make it suitable for structural and hygienic applications where heat resistance and longevity are essential, while copper remains superior for efficient heat transfer. Is Stainless Steel More Biodegradable than Cobalt-Chromium (Co-Cr)? No, stainless steel nor cobalt-chromium (Co-Cr) is biodegradable. Stainless steel and cobalt-chromium are corrosion-resistant and designed for long-term stability, but cobalt-chromium exhibits superior wear resistance and biocompatibility, making it more suitable for permanent medical implants. Stainless steel 316L is used for temporary implants and surgical tools. Stainless steel is fully recyclable, while not biodegradable, allowing efficient recovery and reuse. The Cobalt-Chromium remains the preferred choice in orthopedic and dental applications requiring durability and minimal biological reactivity, whereas stainless steel provides cost-effective performance for short-term medical and structural uses. Does Stainless Steel Perform Better in Low-Temperature Environments than Brass? Yes, austenitic stainless steels (grades 304 and 316) perform better in low-temperature environments than brass because their properties retain strength, toughness, and ductility even under cryogenic conditions. Brass loses ductility and becomes brittle in extreme cold, increasing the risk of cracking under stress. The crystal structure of austenitic stainless steel allows it to absorb impact and mechanical loads without fracture, making it suitable for cryogenic storage tanks, pipelines, and components used in refrigeration and aerospace systems. The material's corrosion resistance further increases performance in low-temperature, moisture-prone environments. The Brass remains useful for moderate temperature applications, but austenitic stainless steel offers superior reliability and mechanical stability under severe cold conditions. Is Stainless Steel More Easily Recycled than 6061 Aluminum Alloy? Yes, stainless steel can be considered easier to recycle than 6061 aluminum alloy, depending on the criteria used. Stainless steel tolerates mixed scrap streams, can be remelted repeatedly without significant loss of mechanical or chemical properties, and is efficiently recovered in large-scale recycling systems. The 6061 aluminum alloy is also highly recyclable, but requires more precise grade separation to maintain its strength and corrosion resistance. Stainless steel’s tolerance for mixed scrap and its stable properties after remelting often make it favorable in heavy industrial recycling environments. Does Stainless Steel Offer More Structural Stability than Titanium in High-Performance Settings? No, stainless steel does not offer more structural stability than titanium in high-performance settings. Titanium has a superior strength-to-weight ratio, maintaining structural integrity under extreme mechanical stress while being lighter than stainless steel (4.5 g/cm³ vs 7.8 g/cm³). Titanium is ideal for aerospace, military, and high-speed automotive applications where weight reduction is critical for performance and efficiency. Stainless steel provides excellent strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance, and even outperforms titanium at very high temperatures in some cases, but its higher density limits its suitability for weight-sensitive designs. Titanium’s combination of high tensile strength, fatigue resistance, and thermal stability gives it a clear advantage in advanced engineering applications requiring performance and lightweight construction. Is Stainless Steel More Resistant to Fatigue than 7075 Aluminum Alloy ? Some stainless steel grades, such as martensitic and precipitation-hardening types, have higher fatigue resistance than 7075 aluminum alloy. Stainless steel’s toughness, dense microstructure, and alloying elements (chromium and nickel) allow it to resist crack initiation and propagation under repeated cyclic loading. Aluminum alloy 7075 is firm and lightweight, but is susceptible to corrosion and surface defects, which reduce its fatigue life. Stainless steel is therefore preferred for components subjected to repeated stress and vibration fasteners, springs, and rotating machinery), where long-term durability under mechanical strain is critical. A stainless steel combination of fatigue resistance, toughness, and corrosion resistance enables superior performance over 7075 Aluminum Alloy in demanding service conditions. title: SupaClub
summary: The Worlds First Software Engineering Nightclub.
body_text: Announcing SupaClub (pronounced “Super-Clurb”), the world’s first Software Engineering Nightclub. Located on the Indonesian island of Bali, SupaClub is where the digital nomads of South East Asia are mixing Hardcore Techno with Hardcore Engineering. In March this year, some members of the Supabase team took advantage of the fact that they can work fully remotely, and spent a week working in Bali. The island is a great place to relax in coffee shops during the day, but when night time rolled around our team faced a major problem - the large established nightclubs of Bali would not allow our engineers to bring their laptops into the club. They have strict rules against EMACS on the dance floor, killing our dream of fixing bugs whilst jamming to 90s club anthems. Our team got together and decided that we would do what we do best at Supabase. We’d ship a fix, and today that fix becomes a reality. SupaClub, situated near the beach in the Canggu neighborhood of Bali, will open its doors this coming Friday. It can house 4000 developers across 4 floors, each with a dedicated DJ and breakout rooms. It has UltraSpeed 1Gbps WiFi and bookable standing desks on every floor. VIP SupaBrew bottle service is available inside private conference rooms, complete with whiteboards and UltraWide monitors for full immersion (Think WeWork-meets-Pacha). In terms of beverage selection, SupaBrew will of course be available behind the bar, along with a cocktail list that includes: Bjarne Pisco Stroustrup - A back-to-basics tantalizing mix of tart, sweet, and silky pisco brandy that won't leave your pointers dangling The Linus - A spicy twist on the Bloody Mary, this aggressive blend will have you shouting for more Mojito-js - we would list the ingredients but our mixologists keep changing the spec HTML Highball - Not a real cocktail, more of a mocktail SupaClub was made possible with the help of infamous Fyre Fest investor Ja Rule and “Super Bass” songstress Niki Minaj, both of which will also be performing on the opening night. If you would like to reserve a spot on the guest list for the opening night please email us at noreply@supabase.com with a link to your GitHub account and "Re: april fools" in the subject line. See you there.

title: Why You Should Transcribe Your Calls
summary: Phone call transcription is the process of converting recorded phone conversations into written words. Learn how to transcribe calls with Plivo.
body_text: Plivo’s Voice API includes a feature you may not be taking full advantage of: call transcription. Call transcription is the process of converting recorded phone conversations into written words. It can help you in a number of ways. With a transcript, anyone can search or visually scan call conversations instead of listening to an entire recording — a process that’s more efficient than voice call monitoring. With phone call transcription you can: Improve agent performance — Managers and agents can search and organize transcribed calls based on outcomes, and learn from them to create best practices documents or knowledge base articles. Transcripts can help you improve grading, quality monitoring, and agent and team performance. They can also help managers develop personalized training objectives for agents to improve their performance over time. Meanwhile, sales agents can learn from transcripts to improve their customer service, as well as identify cross- and upsell opportunities and identify effective ways to move leads further along the pipeline. Reduce training time — You can share transcriptions among reps and during the new-hire onboarding process. They can serve as example scripts that illustrate what a rep should or shouldn’t say to a customer. Do post-facto keyword analytics — Transcripts make it easy to analyze which keywords appear in call conversations and how frequently, so you can learn what your customers are saying and use that information to make better decisions. For instance, if you can understand what aspects and features of a product customers are happy or unhappy about, you can better prioritize efforts to improve the product. Increase accessibility — For the hearing-impaired, transcripts make absorbing information easier. Inclusive practices such providing transcripts are not only good business, they may also be the law. For instance, in the US, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 says, “No otherwise qualified individual with a disability in the United States . . . shall, solely by reason of her or his disability, be excluded from the participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance . . . .” The Office for Civil Rights enforces Section 504 in programs and activities that receive federal financial assistance from the Education Department, including public school districts and institutions of higher education. If your business has a presence in education, transcriptions may be required. Enhance customer experience — For contact centers especially, customer satisfaction is crucial, and the best way to deliver on customer satisfaction is to have customer insights. Call transcripts unlock those insights, giving you an easy-to-review format and high-level perspective, which is especially useful when you have a lot of calls covering a number of subjects. Call transcription makes it simple to review information and discern trends, and identify instances where you should go back and listen to specific calls for more context. The price is right You might be willing to pay a lot to gain all of the benefits of speech-to-text, but with Plivo you don’t have to. Our speech transcription service is surprisingly inexpensive. Plivo charges less than a penny per minute of recorded speech — a fraction of what most cloud communication services charge — which makes it a trivial decision to say yes and gain all of the benefits. However, before you transcribe any calls, make sure that doing so is legal in your locale. Some jurisdictions ban not only transcribing calls but even recording calls, or require informed consent by some or all parties in a conversation. Consult your friendly neighborhood lawyer. How to transcribe calls Now that you know why to use speech-to-text transcription, let’s talk about how: Simply provide an additional parameter to the Record Call API when you initiate a call. The transcription_url parameter defines the webhook URL to which the transcription should be posted. After the call completes, Plivo will post the transcribed text to the URL you specify, along with other parameters about the recording, as you can see on our API documentation page. It’s really that simple and that inexpensive. If you’re already using Plivo’s Voice API but haven’t yet tried transcription, think about places where it might come in handy. If you’d like to get started, sign up for a free trial account and see all that Plivo can do.

title: Heat Sink: Definition, How It Works, Components, Types, and Applications
summary: Learn more about these devices and their purpose.
body_text: How Does a Heat Sink Work? A heat sink makes use of the principles of conductive, convective, and radiative heat transfer to move heat from a hotter source to a lower-temperature fluid. Heat is conducted from this source into the sink. Heat sinks are made from materials with high thermal conductivity, such as copper or aluminum, allowing them to quickly conduct heat away from the source. This heat then transfers from the sink into the surrounding fluid via convection and radiation. The heat transfer rate is increased by having a large surface area in contact with the heat exchange fluid. Surface area can be dramatically increased by cutting fins into the heat sink base material. Depending on cooling demands, heat sinks function either through natural convection (passive cooling) or forced convection provided by a fan or liquid pump (active cooling). What Is the Purpose of a Heat Sink? A heat sink is designed to dissipate waste heat caused by the operation of electrical or mechanical devices. This waste heat can accumulate and cause failures or degrade performance if not removed. What Are the Key Components of a Heat Sink? A heat sink is a relatively simple device. Listed below are the five components that make up a typical heat sink: 1. Base A heat sink base is typically a flat block or sheet of material with excellent thermal conductivity. The base typically has a consistent cross-sectional thickness, but it can also be designed to have a cross-sectional profile that optimizes heat transfer for the specific geometry of the heat source. The base is typically mounted to the heat source with mounting hardware and thermal paste. 2. Fins Fins protruding from the heat sink base are responsible for the transfer of heat to the surrounding fluid. These fins increase the heat sink's surface area in contact with air or coolant, which enhances the rate of heat dissipation. The fins can either form an integral part of the base or can be attached separately using various techniques, for example, via a compression process. The shape and arrangement of the fins can dramatically improve the heat transfer rate. 3. Heat Pipes A heat pipe is designed to transfer heat along its axis. Heat pipes can be incorporated inside standard heat sinks and heat spreaders through press fitting, soldering, and thermally conductive epoxy to improve their heat transfer efficiency. They work by transferring heat via a phase change mechanism that causes fluid to vaporize at the heat source, then travel along the axis of the heat pipe to the point where it cools down and changes back into a liquid via condensation. 4. Thermal Interface Material Thermal interface materials, or thermal pastes, are used to significantly improve heat transfer between the heat source and the base of the heat sink by filling any air voids between the heat source and the heat sink. Air is a poor conductor of heat, so filling air gaps with a more thermally conductive material enhances the cooling efficiency of a heat sink. Thermal pastes can be ceramic, metal-oxide, or silicone-based. Metal-based thermal pastes offer high thermal conductivity but are electrically conductive and should be used with caution near sensitive components. 5. Mounting Hardware Heat sinks can be securely fixed to their target heat sources using a number of different mounting methods. For smaller heat sinks, an adhesive with high thermal conductivity is used to directly stick the heat sink onto a heat source. This method is typically used on smaller PCB components. For larger heat sinks, normal screws can be used, or alternatively, spring-loaded push pins are used to optimize the contact pressure between the heat source and the heat sink. What Materials Are Heat Sinks Made Of? Heat sinks are made from materials with high thermal conductivity. The most common of these are listed below. Aluminum: Aluminum is a lightweight, low-cost material with good thermal conductivity. It is commonly used in heat sinks for electronic devices, such as computers and LED lights. Copper: Copper has excellent thermal conductivity and can be used on more sensitive components like computer CPUs. Aluminum Alloys: Pure aluminum is soft and difficult to machine, so aluminum alloys are often used. High-purity alloys like 1050 retain excellent thermal conductivity, while stronger alloys like 6061 offer improved mechanical strength at the cost of reduced thermal conductivity. Graphite: Certain forms of engineered graphite, like pyrolytic graphite, have very high in-plane thermal conductivity, rivaling or exceeding copper, and are significantly lighter. However, bulk or isotropic graphite has lower thermal performance. Diamond: Diamond has much higher thermal conductivity than copper and is used in specialized semiconductor applications. However, its high cost limits it to niche uses such as high-performance heat spreaders or laser diode cooling. What Are the Types of Heat Sinks? There are three basic types of heat sinks. They are described in more detail below: 1. Passive Heat Sinks A passive heat sink is the simplest type of heat sink. It is simply a base with fins. Heat is transferred primarily through natural convection. As the air around the fins heats up through conduction, the hot air rises, causing cooler air to replace it. This is a continuous process. These types of heat sinks are not the most effective. 2. Hybrid Heat Sinks A hybrid heat sink makes use of a control system to decide when to employ passive or active behavior. When the heat source produces low levels of heat, the fan or pump is not turned on, because natural convection is sufficient to transfer the required amount of heat away from the heat source. When natural convection is not adequate, the fan is activated, and forced convection helps to increase the amount of heat transferred away from the source. 3. Active Heat Sinks An active heat sink makes use of forced convection to transfer heat. When a fan or pump causes fluid flow over the heat sink, this constant flow keeps replacing the hot fluid around the heat sink with cooler fluid. The higher the flow rate, the higher the heat transfer rate. Active heat sinks are more effective than passive heat sinks. What Are the Applications of Heat Sinks? Heat sinks are used wherever waste heat has the potential to damage equipment. Some examples are listed below: 1. Computer Processors Computer processors (CPUs) produce a large amount of waste heat during operation. CPUs often use active cooling systems with copper heat sinks to manage high thermal loads during operation. Cool CPUs can operate more effectively. 2. LED Lighting LED lights don’t emit much radiant heat like incandescent bulbs, but the LED junction itself generates significant thermal energy during operation. This heat must be dissipated, typically through passive heat sinks in smaller LEDs. 3. Power Electronics Power electronics like AC–DC converters generate waste heat from components such as MOSFETs and voltage regulators. Aluminum heat sinks are commonly used in these applications, sometimes combined with active fans for more demanding thermal loads. 4. Automotive Industry Apart from the heat sinks used on the control circuitry of vehicles, heat sinks are also used to keep electric motors cool during operation as well as to cool onboard chargers for electric vehicles. 5. Aerospace Industry Aerospace systems use heat sinks in control circuitry and onboard electronics. In spacecraft, where there is no atmosphere for convection, specialized heat sinks radiate heat into space using high-emissivity surfaces and often include heat pipes to transport heat to radiators. 6. Consumer Electronics Consumer electronics make extensive use of heat sinks to keep devices cool and operating efficiently. Typical examples include the heat sinks in computers and cell phones.

title: Conflito de interesses de fornecedores: quanto impacta sua empresa?
summary: O conflito de interesses de fornecedores gera riscos para sua empresa, até financeiros. Confira como identificar e mitigar esse problema
body_text: O conflito de interesses de fornecedores é uma situação que acontece quando questões pessoais, políticas, familiares, financeiras, entre outras similares, afetam o julgamento e as tomadas de decisões empresariais . Por exemplo, esse comportamento pode acontecer quando um funcionário do time de compras e procurement precisa contratar uma empresa fornecedora e, apesar de ter nas mãos ofertas mais relevantes para o negócio, escolhe a que pertence a um amigo próximo. Neste caso, o interesse particular do profissional passou à frente do que é realmente vantajoso para a empresa na qual trabalha, e essa escolha pode colocá-la em vários riscos. Como você deve estar imaginando, decisões desse tipo afetam seriamente o sucesso e o crescimento de uma companhia. Isso porque, a fim de suprir as conveniências pessoais, comumente critérios como qualidade, credibilidade, tempo de mercado, compliance, preços, e outros, são deixados de lado na hora de contratar um fornecedor. Porém, será que existe uma maneira de evitar isso e proteger o seu negócio? A boa notícia é que sim, existem várias formas de mitigar, ou até mesmo de eliminar conflito de interesses de fornecedores. Continue a leitura deste artigo e confira agora quais são, e o que fazer perante casos desse tipo. O que é conflito de interesses? Conflito de interesses é uma condição na qual o julgamento e as decisões empresariais são afetadas em decorrência de questões e preferências pessoais, a exemplo das familiares, políticas e profissionais, e também devido a potenciais vantagens financeiras. Logo, é possível entender que conflito de interesses de fornecedores é quando o relacionamento e a dinâmica de contratação entre quem fornece e quem recebe insumos e/ou serviços são alterados por conta de conveniências para algum dos envolvidos. Sobre isso, é bem importante que você saiba que esse tipo de embate pode acontecer tanto em esferas públicas quanto nas privadas. No setor público, esse assunto é tratado no artigo 3º da Lei 12.813/2013 , que determina que essa é uma situação gerada pelo confronto entre os interesses públicos e privados, o qual pode afetar o coletivo e/ou influenciar o desempenho de funções públicas. Já no setor privado, o conflito de interesses não conta com regulamentações ou leis específicas. Isso significa que cada empresa tem liberdade para dar suas próprias tratativas, com base em sua cultura e valores. Todavia, esse processo pode ser embasado na NBR ISO 37001 , Norma de Certificação de Sistemas de Gestão de Compliance Antissuborno, que dá às companhias diretrizes de como prevenir, identificar e tratar casos de suborno entre seus agentes, incluindo colaboradores, fornecedores e outros. Confira tudo sobre essa importante norma no artigo: “ O que é ISO 37001: para que serve, vantagens e como implementar ” Exemplos de conflito de interesses de fornecedores Além do exemplo de conflito de interesses de fornecedores que citamos logo na abertura deste artigo, outros que ajudam a entender esse conceito são: receber de um potencial fornecedor vantagens que induzam a contratá-lo, deixando outras opções de lado, por exemplo, almoços, viagens e presentes pessoais; definir critérios técnicos, com base em preferências pessoais, que levem à obrigatoriedade de contratar uma empresa fornecedora específica; contratar negócios fornecedores cujos proprietários são parentes, deixando de avaliar outros que podem estar mais alinhados às necessidades da empresa por esse motivo; contratar um determinado fornecedor por conta da promessa de divisão de ganhos provenientes dessa parceria, tirando a chance de outros que não atuam dessa forma. O que causa conflitos de interesses de fornecedores? Comumente, a causa dos conflitos de interesses de fornecedores é a obtenção de vantagens pessoais . Isto é, sua origem costuma ser a conquista de algum privilégio para uso particular. Justamente por conta dessas motivações é que a mitigação dessa situação está diretamente relacionada a uma norma voltada para medidas antissuborno. Infelizmente, ainda há profissionais que enxergam o relacionamento com fornecedores como um meio para “alcançar patamares mais elevados”, seja de posição dentro da empresa, seja financeiro. Por conta disso, é fundamental que os gestores adotem ações para identificar e evitar esse tipo de comportamento, tão prejudicial para a dinâmica do negócio. Somada a essas causas, há outra que pode fomentar o conflito de interesses com empresas fornecedoras. No caso, estamos falando da existência de algum tipo de relação pessoal dos colaboradores concorrentes . Imagine que seu negócio precise contratar um novo software para gestão de fornecedores . Na busca pelo melhor do mercado, o profissional responsável por essa tarefa encontra dois: um que atende absolutamente todas as necessidades da empresa, e outro no qual a cônjuge trabalha, mas que não é tão completo. Ainda que não haja benefício financeiro direto, ao levar para os gestores a segunda opção como a mais indicada, esse colaborador estará gerando um conflito de interesse entre o que a companhia precisa, e o que ele julga mais conveniente. Ou seja, a percepção pessoal do colaborador interferiu diretamente na tomada de decisão empresarial. E, como já comentamos, isso pode gerar uma série de impactos para o negócio. Quais são os impactos para as empresas contratantes? E por falar em impactos, os principais que uma empresa pode sofrer, decorrente de conflito de interesse de negócios fornecedores, são: comprometer a dinâmica interna, a cultura e o clima organizacional; perder qualidade em matéria-prima, insumos e//ou serviços contratados; lidar com companhias que não estão em compliance e sofrer reflexos de problemas legais, financeiros, fiscais, contábeis e outros semelhantes; vincular a imagem da marca a negociações e comportamentos antiéticos; envolver, ainda que indiretamente, a organização em crimes como fraudes, corrupção, lavagem de dinheiro e outros; trazer para sua base fornecedores que usam mão de obra escrava e/ou trabalho infantil; pagar valores altos e incompatíveis com o que está sendo entregue. Como identificar e mitigar conflito de interesses de fornecedores? Uma das melhores maneiras de identificar conflito de interesses em sua rede de abastecimento é por meio da realização de auditorias internas e externas . Ao fazer isso, você verifica, pontualmente, se os processos adotados para contratar fornecedores estão adequados e, principalmente, de acordo com os parâmetros legais esperados. Outra forma de fazer essa identificação é criando um canal de denúncias que pode ser usado com segurança e discrição por todos os seus stakeholders. Já para mitigar problemas desse tipo, algumas das boas práticas que podem ser adotadas são: criar políticas internas e oferecer treinamentos adequados aos funcionários; elaborar um código de conduta de fornecedores com as regras e padrões éticos que precisam ser seguidos para que a parceria seja continuada; automatizar o processo de busca e de homologação de fornecedores, para que todas as etapas sejam feitas automaticamente, nenhum documento deixe de ser solicitado ou analisado, e também como forma de evitar a influência direta de um profissional nessas tratativas. Como a Linkana pode ajudar sua empresa? Nesse último quesito, a Linkana pode ajudar sua empresa, porque somos a primeira fundação de dados de fornecedores compartilhada do Brasil . Nossa base de dados de perfis universais de fornecedores permite que compradores busquem, analisem e homologuem fornecedores em alguns cliques. Com isso, aceleramos radicalmente processos de onboarding, de análise e de monitoramento de fornecedores — graças aos dados dos fornecedores já preenchidos por eles ou por outra empresa —, permitindo o uso de dados e insights compartilhados entre as maiores corporações do Brasil. title: MyMD Pharmaceuticals® Provides Dosing Update on Phase 2 Multi-Center Clinical Trial of MYMD-1® as a Therapy for Delaying Aging and Extending Healthy Lifespan

body_text: MyMD Pharmaceuticals® Provides Dosing Update on Phase 2 Multi-Center Clinical Trial of MYMD-1® as a Therapy for Delaying Aging and Extending Healthy Lifespan April 12, 2023 8:30am EDT Download as PDF - Currently, there are no FDA-approved treatments for sarcopenia/frailty - - MyMD is only 3 patients away from dosing its final patient in its first Phase 2 clinical trial of lead drug candidate MYMD-1® - BALTIMORE, MD--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- MyMD Pharmaceuticals, Inc . ® (Nasdaq: MYMD) (“MyMD” or “the Company”), a clinical stage biopharmaceutical company developing groundbreaking therapies for the treatment of serious and debilitating autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, today announced a dosing update on its fully-funded Phase 2 clinical trial of lead drug candidate MYMD-1®, an orally available next-generation TNF-alpha inhibitor, as a therapy for chronic inflammation associated with sarcopenia and frailty ( NCT05283486 ). The Safety Review Committee has confirmed no safety or toxicity issues with the first 30 patients enrolled in this study and has voted unanimously to escalate to the final dose level. Thirty patients enrolled in Cohorts 1, 2, and 3 have completed dosing and end of study visits. To date, three subjects from Cohort 4 have completed end of study visits. There are no outstanding study visits and all 30 patients have officially completed all study parameters and been discharged from the study. “We are proud of the notable progress that we have made thus far on our first Phase 2 study of MYMD-1,” said Chris Chapman MD, President, Director, and Chief Medical Officer at MyMD Pharmaceuticals. “As we move into the final cohort of this study, we remain hopeful in MYMD-1’s potential to transform future treatment of sarcopenia/frailty in the aging population.” The Phase 2 multi-center double-blind, placebo controlled, randomized study ( NCT05283486 ) is currently ongoing to investigate the efficacy, tolerability and pharmacokinetics of MYMD-1 in the treatment of chronic inflammation associated with sarcopenia/frailty inpatients aged 65 years or older. The study’s primary objective is to demonstrate reduction of chronic inflammatory markers in patients treated with MYMD-1® versus placebo. To qualify for the clinical trial, patients’ biomarkers during the screening period must be within the following criteria: IL-6 ≥ 2.5pg/mL; and/or sTNFR-1 ≥ 1500pg/mL. To date, MyMD has randomized and dosed 37 of 40 total patients across Cohorts 1 (n=10; 600mg), 2 (n=10; 750mg), 3 (n=10; 900mg) and 4 (n=7; 1050mg). On average, it is estimated that 5 to 13% of elderly people between the ages of 60 and 70 are affected by sarcopenia. These numbers increase to 11 to 50% for those aged 80 or above.1 Currently, there are no FDA approved treatments for chronic inflammation associated with sarcopenia/frailty for those aged 65 years or older. “The aging disorders market is expected to be at least $600 billion by 20252,” continued Dr. Chapman. “TNF-α blockers are the most prescribed drugs by revenue, a global market of approximately $40 billion per year.3 Studies have shown that a slowdown in aging that increases life expectancy by one year is worth $38 trillion and by 10 years is worth $367 trillion.4” MYMD-1 ® is an oral next-generation TNF-α inhibitor with the potential to transform the way that TNF-α based diseases are treated due to its selectivity and ability to cross the blood brain barrier. MyMD is planning early-stage trials for rheumatoid arthritis and will provide guidance as the program develops. About MyMD Pharmaceuticals MyMD Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Nasdaq: MYMD), is a clinical stage biopharma company developing groundbreaking therapies for the treatment of serious and debilitating autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. MyMD’s lead clinical candidate, MYMD-1 ® , is an orally available next-generation TNF-α inhibitor with the potential to transform the way that TNF-α based diseases are treated. MYMD-1 ® , with its small molecule design, improved safety profile and ability to cross the blood brain barrier, has the promise to provide meaningful therapeutic solutions to patients not served by current TNF-α inhibitors and as a potential therapy for CNS-based inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. MYMD-1 ® has demonstrated the potential to slow the aging process and extend healthy lifespan. The company is evaluating MYMD-1 ® in Phase 2 studies for sarcopenia/frailty, a result of the aging process, as well as early-stage trials for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), with the potential to expand into other applications. MyMD’s second therapeutic candidate is Supera-CBD, a novel, synthetic, non-toxic cannabidiol (CBD) analog that is 8000 times more potent a CB2 agonist (activator) than plant-based CBD. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA)’s scientific review concluded Supera-CBD will not be considered a controlled substance or listed chemical under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) and its governing regulations or require scheduling during development . In addition to its potential role in managing addiction, anxiety, chronic pain and seizures, Supera-CBD has also been shown to have anti-inflammatory effects. title: 6 estrategias clave para el reclutamiento masivo
summary: El reclutamiento masivo puede ser una tarea desafiante y demandante para los reclutadores. A continuación, aprende cómo dominarlo y alcanzar el éxito.
body_text: 6 estrategias clave para el reclutamiento masivo Para las empresas que necesitan una gran cantidad de trabajadores operativos, el reclutamiento implica un esfuerzo constante. Necesitan encontrar personal calificado para que las operaciones diarias funcionen sin problemas. Llevar adelante un proceso de reclutamiento masivo sin las herramientas y estrategias adecuadas puede convertirse en una tarea difícil y que demanda mucho tiempo. A continuación, desarrollaremos este concepto comenzando por los principales desafíos que enfrentarás en el reclutamiento masivo, seguido por estrategias clave y, finalmente, métricas que puedes utilizar para facilitar el proceso de reclutamiento. ¿Qué es el reclutamiento masivo? Contratar a más de 500 personas por año es considerado de alto volumen. Sin embargo, en algunas áreas, superar las 250 contrataciones anuales tiene el mismo significado. Por lo general, podrás ver estos números en industrias con mayor demanda o rotación como retail, restaurantes y producción en masa con miles de empleados. El reclutamiento masivo también se da en empresas que están contratando para nuevas instalaciones. ¿Cuál es la diferencia entre el reclutamiento masivo y otros tipos de reclutamiento? El reclutamiento puede dividirse en varias categorías. Por un lado, existe el reclutamiento ejecutivo, que se enfoca en encontrar a candidatos indicados para niveles ejecutivos. En cambio, el reclutamiento masivo es otra categoría que se refiere al reclutamiento de muchos candidatos en un corto período de tiempo. En ocasiones, se suele confundir esta categoría con la del reclutamiento corporativo. Este último, en vez de enfocarse en cubrir muchas vacantes en poco tiempo, busca llenar vacantes de posiciones especializadas. Desafíos comunes en el reclutamiento masivo Dado que esta categoría de reclutamiento implica trabajar con un gran número de candidatos, se entiende al reclutamiento masivo como un negocio cambiante. A continuación, encontrarás un resumen de los tres desafíos más grandes: Muchas aplicaciones Si contratas 500 personas o más, estamos hablando de 500 o más aplicaciones ¿verdad? Incorrecto. Considera tu ratio de candidatos a contratar , que mide la cantidad de aplicantes que recibes, con la cantidad de contrataciones que realizas con ese pool de talento. Raramente, el ratio de candidatos a contratar es 1:1. Incluso, un ratio de 2:1 significa filtrar 1000 aplicaciones para hacer 500 contrataciones. Mala experiencia para los candidatos El reclutamiento masivo es desafiante de por sí, pero se hace aún más difícil si los candidatos dicen haber sufrido una experiencia negativa. Cuando los candidatos tienen una mala experiencia durante el proceso de reclutamiento de una empresa, es probable que retiren su candidatura y sigan buscando por otro lado. O peor, pueden hablar con sus colegas o amigos, lo cual podría llevar a una mala reputación y una baja en las aplicaciones en general de aquella empresa. Proceso manuales y repetitivos La velocidad es fundamental cuando tu compañía necesita atraer un gran número de empleados nuevos de forma rápida. Las tareas manuales desactualizadas retrasan el proceso de reclutamiento, y esto afecta directamente a la productividad de tu empresa. 6 estrategias clave para el reclutamiento masivo Cuando se trata de un gran volumen de candidatos, es indispensable que tu proceso de reclutamiento cuente con estrategias eficientes. Utiliza las siguientes seis estrategias para atraer candidatos de calidad y así, impulsar y mejorar tu proceso de reclutamiento masivo. 1. Ofrecer aplicaciones de fácil acceso El tiempo de los candidatos es valioso. Suelen aplicar a muchos empleos a la vez, por lo tanto, pocos tendrán la paciencia para completar aplicaciones que sean largas y complejas. Si tu proceso de aplicación es difícil de encontrar en tu sitio web o consiste en formularios de muchas páginas, los candidatos pueden perder interés y avanzar con aplicaciones más dinámicas en otras empresas. Es por eso que necesitas hacer que tu proceso de aplicación sea de fácil acceso. Evita la tentación de incluir formularios largos. Ofrece un proceso simple para que los candidatos sean más propensos a completarlas y enviar sus solicitudes. Asimismo, cada vez más candidatos son usuarios de dispositivos móviles. Por ende, es más probable que completen su proceso de aplicación si tienen la posibilidad de aplicar con códigos QR, SMS, redes sociales u otras opciones que no requieran de una dirección de correo electrónico. Si tu portal de empleo es apto para dispositivos móviles, ayudas a que los usuarios puedan aplicar en dónde sea que estén, en lugar de tener que esperar a sentarse en una computadora. También deberías asegurarte de que tu sitio web sea fácil de encontrar y que no obligue a los candidatos a atravesar distintos pasos para enviar sus solicitudes. 2. Promocionar el empleo en donde los candidatos puedan verlo Una encuesta realizada en el 2019 por Jobvite, Job Seeker Nation Survey , arroja la siguientes estadísticas: El 69% de los candidatos busca vacantes en bolsas o portales de empleo. Casi la mitad de los candidatos conocen vacantes de boca en boca. El 41% busca empleos en redes sociales. El 37% utiliza redes profesionales para enterarse de ofertas laborales. Si quieres atraer un gran volumen de candidatos, debes promocionar los empleos en donde las personas lo vayan a ver. Comienza por bolsas de empleo, como Indeed o Simply Hired, y redes sociales, como Facebook, donde lo verán cientos de candidatos calificados a la vez. (Consejo: sabías que alrededor de 5 mil millones de personas utilizan redes sociales? Aprovéchalo para conocer a tus candidatos). Puedes impulsar el boca en boca implementando un programa de referidos entre tus empleados. Esto no sólo da a conocer tus vacantes, sino que también es una buena forma de que tus empleados traigan candidatos nuevos de su red de contactos, lo cual aumenta la calidad de los mismos. 3. Utilizar una herramienta de reclutamiento automatizado Al desarrollar un proyecto, necesitas las herramientas correctas para llevarlo adelante de manera exitosa. No intentarías construir un rascacielos con solo un martillo y clavos, ¿verdad? La misma lógica se aplica para el reclutamiento masivo y, en este caso, el equipamiento que utilizan los profesionales de RRHH incluye plataformas como Emi, que optimizan el proceso para que tus gerentes y equipos de reclutamiento puedan manejar un alto volumen de candidatos. Con Emi, puedes automatizar la publicación de empleos para que, cuando tengas una vacante, la plataforma envíe descripciones de empleo y otros detalles a tus sitios de trabajo y redes sociales de preferencia. También puede ayudarte a ordenar y filtrar aplicaciones, y buscar con palabras claves para reducir el pool de candidatos. Además, tendrás la posibilidad de evaluar la eficiencia de tus campañas, facilitar el onboarding y más. 4. Optimizar tus descripciones de empleo Existen múltiples razones por las cuales es fundamental optimizar el contenido que los candidatos reciben. Para empezar, como en las campañas de marketing, mejorar tu campaña de reclutamiento puede aumentar el alcance para atraer mejor talento. El contenido optimizado también ayuda a prevenir dolores de cabeza. Por ejemplo, los candidatos pueden aplicar a un empleo con una descripción no muy específica y averiguar, en la mitad del proceso de entrevistas, que no es lo que esperaban. Sé claro con las responsabilidades, expectativas, beneficios y salario para evitar perder el tiempo con cuestiones como estas. Otras cuestiones, como preguntas específicas, pueden ayudarte a filtrar candidatos rápidamente entre aquellos que dan una respuesta deseable y aquellos que no. El contenido optimizado, a su vez, ayuda a mejorar la calidad de las contrataciones, porque da una idea general de la cultura empresarial. A medida que los candidatos leen avisos y publicaciones de empleo, se evalúan a sí mismos en torno a si consideran que podrían encajar con la cultura mencionada o no. Por ende, es importante describirla de forma precisa. 5. Mejorar la experiencia de los candidatos Considera la búsqueda de empleo de la misma forma en la que consideras ir de compras. Si estás buscando empleo, de alguna forma, estás yendo de compras y, una mala experiencia de atención al cliente es una de las razones por las cuales buscarías comprar en otro sitio. Lo mismo sucede cuando los candidatos tienen una mala experiencia en su proceso de aplicación o experiencia de reclutamiento. El hecho de manejar un gran volumen de candidatos no es una razón para descuidar la calidad de su proceso. Brinda una experiencia personalizada, sé atento al responder preguntas y asegúrate de que los candidatos tengan acceso a todo lo necesario para aplicar y continuar con las entrevistas. Así es como lograrás reclutar con empatía . 6. Medir y evaluar métricas El mundo de los negocios modernos funciona con información. Así como necesitas datos en marketing para vender productos efectivamente, o información contable para alinear presupuestos, necesitas hacer seguimiento de tus métricas de reclutamiento. Esto mantiene el proceso de atracción de talento en funcionamiento, y te ayuda a modificar dicho proceso de manera contínua para obtener mejores resultados. De hecho, existen algunas métricas de reclutamiento fundamentales y ampliaremos dicha información a continuación. Las métricas más importantes para supervisar el éxito de tu proceso de reclutamiento masivo Las métricas son una parte fundamental de tu estrategia: pueden ayudar a tu equipo de reclutamiento a mejorar en la toma de decisiones y en la efectividad de su trabajo. Las métricas más importantes a tener en cuenta son las siguientes: Ratio de aplicantes a contratar Como hemos mencionado anteriormente, si tienes un ratio alto para tu industria, no dejes de revisar tus fuentes, proceso de aplicación o proceso de entrevistas, para ver qué puedes mejorar con el objetivo de equilibrar este ratio. Candidatos por fuente Esta métrica mide el número de candidatos que cada fuente trae, permitiendo que pongas más foco en tus fuentes más productivas. Contrataciones por fuente Así mismo, puedes utilizar esta métrica con la misma finalidad, que es identificar qué fuentes son las más efectivas para tu empresa. Asegúrate de comparar esta métrica con candidatos por fuente. Puedes hacerlo creando un ratio de aplicantes a contratar por fuente. Por ejemplo, si una fuente trae un ratio de 100 candidatos por contratación y otro trae dos, puedes decidir si un ratio de 100:1 vale la pena. Tasa de conversión Como el ratio de aplicantes a contratar, la tasa de conversión indica cuántos candidatos pasan a ser empleados en la empresa. Las tasas de conversión altas son excelentes, pero una tasa de conversión baja puede indicar que necesitas revisar cuestiones como procesos de reclutamiento largos o complicados, los cuales pueden estar desalentando a los candidatos. Presta atención al punto de abandono en el proceso de reclutamiento para identificar en dónde pueden haber problemas, y así modificarlos con el objetivo de lograr mayor conversión. Ratio de aplicantes a entrevistar Este número mide cuántos candidatos avanzan a la primera entrevista. Lo utilizas para conocer detalles importantes de tu proceso de aplicación que puedan estar causando que los solicitantes abandonen el proceso antes de llegar a la entrevista. Ratio de entrevista a contratación Utiliza esta métrica para evaluar el proceso de entrevistas en sí mismo. Supongamos que estás entrevistando a muchos candidatos, pero haciendo pocas contrataciones. Esto podría indicar que estás seleccionando a muchos candidatos para entrevistar, o puede haber otra cuestión como un proceso de entrevistas complejo que ahuyenta a los aplicantes. Puntaje de satisfacción de candidatos Utiliza encuestas y herramientas similares para generar un puntaje de satisfacción. Una vez que sepas cuán satisfechas (o no) están las personas con tu proceso de aplicación y reclutamiento, podrás identificar y solucionar problemas dentro del proceso. Motivos de rechazo Asegúrate de hablar con los candidatos que rechacen una oferta de empleo para entender por qué decidieron no unirse a tu equipo y registra los motivos. Esto puede ayudarte a entender qué partes de tu proceso de reclutamiento necesitan ser modificadas o mejoradas. Asimismo, habla con los entrevistadores y gerentes de reclutamiento acerca de los candidatos que no avanzaron en el proceso y toma nota. Si tu empresa rechaza un gran número de candidatos, esto puede ayudarte a identificar patrones y ajustar tus procesos para filtrar mejor a los candidatos. Ahorrarás tiempo para tu empresa y para los candidatos. Pasos del proceso de aplicación El proceso debería tener tres pasos: Filtro: filtra aplicaciones y CVs para seleccionar el mejor talento y avanzar con el proceso de entrevistas. Entrevistas: se presentan como la oportunidad para que tu equipo de RRHH conozca a los candidatos y seleccione a los mejores. Ofertas: envía ofertas después de que RRHH haya seleccionado el mejor talento de los entrevistados. Haz un seguimiento de la cantidad de personas que atraviesan cada etapa de tu proceso, ya que los números pueden ser reveladores. Por ejemplo, si tienes muchas ofertas rechazadas, puede significar que hay algo poco atractivo en el empleo en sí mismo. Otro ejemplo puede ser que, si tienes un gran número de personas que no continúan con el proceso de entrevistas, puede ser un indicador de que existen problemas en esta etapa. Tiempo de contratación Los tiempos de contrataciones largos pueden ser malos indicadores. En primer lugar, tendrán un costo más alto para las horas de recursos humanos de tu empresa y, dado que muchos de los candidatos quieren convertirse en empleados rápidamente, un tiempo de contratación más largo puede desalentar a los candidatos calificados. Costo por contratación Esto mide los costos de las horas de trabajo, materiales de marketing, valor de publicidad, capacitaciones y más. Mide esta métrica para mantener tus costos bajos.
